In discussion with @kelleyk, we agreed that the scope should be limited to content that's retrieved by the AI system, e.g., via a RAG index or tool call, and not for individual assets being provided by the user to the AI system. The intent is to include:
The user provides a description (e.g., the Google homepage as in the Does direct provision include URLs? #249 example) that the AI system resolves to a URL
The user provides a description that potentially resolves to multiple assets (e.g., "Wikipedia pages describing the countries of Europe")
and to exclude:
The user provides the asset directly to the AI system (e.g., through file upload)
The user provides a URL to an asset that the AI system fetches
The AI system offers to the user to include a specific asset (a URL) as possible input, as part of the user's conversation with the AI system, and the user confirms providing that link as input (either by clicking the link or responding affirmatively in the conversation)

chat.text: On #257: no carve-out needed. (1) Under #249, content a user hands to their own assistive tool should be outside ai-use. #258's "user-chosen input" covers it. chat.author: monicawestin
chat.text:
Lila, I think there's a meaningful distinction in the world of scholarly publishing and library usage standards. Libraries rely heavily on COUNTER usage metrics to evaluate subscriptions, including calculating cost per use. Distinguishing between human and agentic activity matters enormously for understanding how content is actually being used and ensuring those metrics remain meaningful.
COUNTER has recently introduced guidance for reporting agentic AI usage separately, while recognising it as legitimate usage. That distinction isn't about charging AI companies or denying that an agent can act on behalf of a human. It's about ensuring we can measure different forms of engagement accurately.
